title: Re-grouting and resealing a tiled shower enclosure
subtitle: Rake out failed grout and silicone, apply fresh grout to the tile joints, and reseal the corner and base joints to restore a watertight shower
excerpt: How to re-grout and reseal a tiled shower cubicle. Covers raking out old grout, cleaning the joints, applying new tile grout, and replacing silicone sealant at the floor and corner joints.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade practice for wet-area maintenance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cement-based or epoxy filler pressed into the joints between tiles. Cement-based grout is used for most domestic tiling; epoxy grout is harder, more stain-resistant, and used in heavy commercial and wet areas. Available in unsanded (for joints up to 3 mm) and sanded (for joints 3-12 mm) versions.

A flexible, waterproof sealant used at movement joints in wet areas: the junctions between the shower tray and the wall tiles, and at internal vertical corners in a shower. Contains a fungicide to resist mould growth. Available in white, grey, and clear. Never use standard decorator's caulk in a shower; it is not flexible or fungicide-treated.

content.text: Shower grout and silicone fail over time: the grout cracks and absorbs staining, the silicone goes black with mould. Re-grouting the tile joints and replacing the silicone at the floor and corners brings the shower back to watertight. Allow a full day: rake out in the morning, regrout and seal in the afternoon, leave overnight before using.
Rake out the old grout and silicone
Use a grout rake (a purpose-made carbide-tipped tool) or a utility knife blade to score and scrape the old

out of the joints. Work in one direction to avoid prying the tile edges. Remove to a depth of about 2 mm. For the silicone joints at the tray edge and vertical corners, cut along both sides of the bead with the utility knife and pull the whole strip away. Clean out any residue with a silicone remover and a scraper; leftover silicone prevents the new sealant bonding. Vacuum the joints and wipe with a damp cloth.

Mix the tile grout to a smooth paste with water. Force it into the joints with a grout float or a filling knife, pressing diagonally across the joints to fill each one fully. Work in sections of about 0.5 square metres. Once the joints are filled, draw the float diagonally across the tiles to remove excess. Wipe with a barely-damp sponge in circular strokes; do not flood the joints with water. Buff off the haze with a dry cloth after 30 to 60 minutes. Leave the grout to set for at least 24 hours before applying silicone at the corner joints.
Reseal the corner and tray joints
Apply painter's masking tape to both tile faces on each side of the joint, leaving a gap of about 4 mm. This ensures a clean, straight bead. Apply a continuous bead of

along the joint. Tool the bead with a wet finger in one smooth stroke, pressing it into the joint and leaving a slightly concave surface. Pull the masking tape away immediately, before the silicone skins. Allow the silicone to cure for at least 24 hours before using the shower.

attrs.symptom: New grout develops black mould within a few months
attrs.cause: Poor ventilation in the shower room, or the shower is not dried down after use.
attrs.fix: Improve extraction (upgrade the extractor fan or run it longer after showering). Wipe the shower walls dry after each use. Use an anti-mould grout spray as a maintenance treatment.

attrs.symptom: The silicone bead peels away from the tray joint after a few weeks
attrs.cause: Silicone applied over residual old silicone, or the tray/tile edge was not fully dry and clean at the time of sealing.
attrs.fix: Remove the failed bead completely, prepare the surface with a silicone remover, ensure the joint is bone dry, and reseal.
